segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation from love, any sharing in the Spirit, any tenderness and compassion,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: make my joy complete: be of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul, of one mind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty conceit, but in humility consider one another as above yourselves,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: each of you looking not to your own interests but also to the interests of others.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Have this mind among yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to exploit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in the likeness of human beings. And being found in appearance as a human being,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only as in my presence but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do everything without grumbling or arguing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine like stars in the world,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: holding fast the word of life, so that on the day of Christ I may boast that I did not run for nothing or labor for nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But even if I am being poured out as a drink offering over the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and I rejoice with all of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way you too should rejoice, and rejoice with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may take heart when I learn how things are with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I have no one like-minded who will genuinely care how things are with you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you know his proven character: as a child with a father he has served as a slave alongside me for the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how things will go with me,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and I am confident in the Lord that I myself will also come soon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I consider it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and coworker and fellow soldier, and your envoy and servant to my need,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since he has been longing for all of you and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And indeed he was ill, close to death. But God had mercy on him, and not on him only but on me also, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I am sending him all the more eagerly, so that you may rejoice at seeing him again and I may have less sorrow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So welcome him in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because for the work of Christ he came close to the point of death, risking his life to make up for what was lacking in your service to me.

notes.phrase: which was also in Christ Jesus
notes.traditional: which was also in Christ Jesus
notes.note: The Greek has no verb in this clause, so one must be supplied. The traditional reading, followed here, supplies 'was' and makes Christ's own attitude the model. Many scholars instead supply 'you have', giving 'think among yourselves the way you do in Christ Jesus', that is, as befits people who belong to him.

The word normally means the visible shape or appearance by which something is recognised. Whether Paul means divine nature, divine glory, or divine status here is disputed, and some translations paraphrase as 'in very nature God'. The same word returns in 'the form of a slave', so one English word is kept for both. Verses 6 to 11 are widely thought to be an early Christian hymn or poem that Paul quotes or composes.

notes.traditional: robbery; a thing to be grasped
notes.note: Older versions have 'thought it not robbery', and many modern ones 'a thing to be grasped', which can suggest snatching at something not yet possessed. Studies of the Greek idiom 'to consider something a harpagmos' indicate it means treating something one already has as an advantage to be used for oneself. This is now the majority scholarly view, though the word is rare and the older readings still have defenders.

notes.traditional: made himself of no reputation; made himself nothing
notes.note: The Greek says simply that he 'emptied himself' and does not say of what. Most interpreters take the phrases that follow, taking a slave's form and being born human, as the explanation, so that the emptying is a self-lowering and not the surrender of some attribute. The literal rendering is kept because it echoes the 'empty conceit' of verse 3.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by another, and not for a hired servant. The contrast in the poem is between the highest status and the lowest. The related verb in verse 22 is rendered 'served as a slave' for the same reason.

Verses 10 and 11 echo Isaiah 45:23, where Israel's God declares that every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance to him. 'Lord' is the word the Greek Scriptures used in place of God's own name, so most interpreters take 'the name above every name' to be 'Lord'. The poem thus applies to Jesus language that Isaiah used of God alone.

The phrase comes from Deuteronomy 32:5 in the Greek version, where Moses describes Israel in the wilderness. The 'grumbling' of verse 14 recalls the same story. The word rendered 'stars' is the one used for the heavenly lights in the Greek of Genesis 1, and the image may also echo Daniel 12:3. Traditional versions have 'lights in the world'.

The verb can mean either to hold on to something or to hold it out to others. 'Holding fast the word of life' fits the context of perseverance. 'Holding out the word of life' fits the image of shining in the world. Translations and commentators are divided.

notes.phrase: poured out as a drink offering
notes.traditional: offered; poured out as a drink offering
notes.note: In both Jewish and Greco-Roman worship, wine was poured out beside or over a sacrifice to complete it. Paul pictures the Philippians' faith as the main sacrifice and his own life, possibly his death, as the libation added to it.

'Gospel' has become a purely religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between 'good news' and 'gospel'.

The Greek word is the one elsewhere translated 'apostle'. Here it has its ordinary sense of a delegate sent on behalf of others, since Epaphroditus was sent by the Philippian church with their gift for Paul. Most translations have 'messenger'. 'Envoy' is chosen because he was commissioned to represent them, not merely to carry word.

The Greek verb is in a past tense, as is 'consider' in verse 25. Ancient letter writers often wrote from the standpoint of the reader, for whom the sending would be past when the letter arrived. Epaphroditus was most likely the bearer of this letter, so English uses the present.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the whole New Testament and translators divide between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant'; the verb δουλεύω (v. 22) should follow the same decision.
Frequent in Paul, Acts and 1 John and variously rendered 'fellowship', 'participation', 'partnership', 'communion' and 'sharing', which hides that one word is in play.

candidates.rendering: be of ... mind / have this mind
candidates.reason: A key Pauline verb, especially in Philippians and Romans, rendered 'think', 'set the mind on', 'have a mindset' and 'be minded'; cross-chapter consistency needs one policy.
With λειτουργός and λειτουργέω it recurs in Luke, Acts, Paul and Hebrews, and translators vary between 'service', 'ministry', 'priestly service' and 'worship'.
The non-technical sense of a church delegate (here and 2 Corinthians 8:23) needs a fixed rendering distinct from 'apostle'.
